name: Mahavira
info: Mahavira, born Vardhamana, was an Indian religious reformer of the 6th or 5th century BCE, whom Jains hold to be the 24th and last Tirthankara of the present time cycle, and who is remembered for teaching ahimsa.

facts.born: Traditionally in 599 BCE at Kundagrama in the Kingdom of the Videhas, in present-day Bihar, to King Siddhartha of the Nāya tribe and Queen Trishala
facts.died: Traditionally at Pawapuri in Bihar, in 527 BCE according to the Śvetāmbaras and 510 BCE according to the Digambaras; some scholars date his death much later
facts.role: Held by Jains to be the 24th and final Tirthankara of the present time cycle; described by historians as a reformer of an existing Jain community, the Niganthas
facts.known: Teaching the five vows; ahimsa as the supreme virtue; the soul and karma; anekantavada; twelve and a half years of asceticism; the four-fold order of monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen

t: Jains hold that Mahavira, born a prince, abandoned royal life at about thirty, practised severe asceticism for twelve and a half years, attained Kevala Jnana, and then preached for thirty years.
He taught five vows, non-violence first among them, and a doctrine of many-sided reality, and Jains hold that his chief disciple Gautama Swami compiled his teachings as the Agamas.
Scholars agree that he lived, but they disagree about his dates, and they see him as a reformer of an older Jain or proto-Jain community led by Parshvanatha, not as its founder.
dyk: In 1974, for the 2,500th anniversary of Mahavira's nirvana, the mendicants of the Śvētāmbara, Digambara and Sthānakavāsī sects for the first time assembled on one platform and agreed on a common flag and emblem.
ev: Traditional date of Mahavira's birth at Kundagrama, as both Jain sects hold
He abandons royal life and becomes a naked ascetic, according to the Ācārāṅga Sūtra

sections.early:
Mahavira, whose birth name was Vardhamana, is placed by Jains in a long line of Tirthankaras, ford-makers who found a passage across the sea of birth and death. He is the 24th and last of the present time cycle. Jain texts describe 26 earlier births, in which he was among other things a denizen of hell, a lion, a god, and Marichi, the son of Bharata Chakravartin.

Jain tradition says he was born in 599 BCE at Kundagrama in the Kingdom of the Videhas, to King Siddhartha of the Nāya tribe and Queen Trishala. The Nāyas were kshatriyas, and the Ācārāṅga Sūtra calls Mahavira a prince of Videha. Where Kundagrama lay in Bihar is disputed: J. P. Sharma identified it as a suburb of Vaishali, and another candidate is the village of Basu Kund, north of Patna.

The Śvetāmbara texts tell that his embryo first formed in a Bamana woman and was moved to Trishala's womb, a story the Digambaras do not accept. The two traditions also differ about his marriage. The Digambaras say he refused to marry Yashoda, while the Śvetāmbaras say he married her and had a daughter, Priyadarshana. His parents were, according to the Ācārāṅga Sūtra, lay followers of Parshvanatha.
sections.rise:
At about thirty, some accounts say twenty-eight, Mahavira left his family and royal life. He undertook severe fasts and bodily mortifications, meditated under the Ashoka tree and discarded his clothes. The Ācārāṅga Sūtra gives a graphic description of his hardships.

According to traditional accounts, he attained Kevala Jnana, omniscience, under a Sāla tree on the bank of the River Rijuvalika near Jrimbhikagrama, after twelve years of rigorous penance, at the age of 43. The Śvētāmbara tradition says he then travelled through India to teach for thirty years, while the Digambaras believe he stayed in his Samavasarana, the holy assembly, and delivered sermons there.

Jain texts name eleven Brahmanas as his first disciples, the eleven Ganadharas, led by Indrabhuti Gautama. Mahavira initiated his mendicants with the five vows. According to the Kalpa Sūtra, he had 14,000 male ascetics, 36,000 female ascetics, 159,000 male lay followers and 318,000 female lay followers. Tradition names Srenika and Kunika, popularly known as Bimbisara and Ajatashatru, and Chetaka of Videha as royal followers, and holds Chandana to be the leader of the female monastic order.
sections.deeds:
Mahavira is best remembered for teaching that ahimsa, non-violence, is the supreme moral virtue. It applies to actions, speech and thought, and extends to every living being, since injuring any being creates bad karma. The Ācārāṅga Sūtra says that he saw life in animals, plants, insects, water, fire and wind, and taught that a monk should not light a fire or wave his arms in the air, lest he injure beings in those states of matter.

With it, the Jain Agamas list four more vows that ascetics and householders observe: satya, truthfulness; asteya, non-stealing; brahmacharya, chastity for monks and faithfulness for householders; and aparigraha, non-attachment, which for mendicants means owning nothing. The Digambara sky-clad ascetics read nakedness as the sign of that vow.

He taught that the soul exists, is substantial and eternal, and is bound to samsara by karma, that there is no creator deity, and that liberation is reached by self-awareness, self-cultivation and restraint. He also taught anekantavada, many-sided reality: truth has many aspects, and language expresses only one perspective at a time. Jain tradition holds that his teachings were compiled by Gautama Swami in twelve parts.
sections.opponents:
Mahavira taught among rival traditions. Early Buddhist texts mention the Niganthas, the community he is thought to have reformed, and Buddhist sources make him a contemporary of the Buddha, in the reigns of Bimbisara and Ajatashatru. Each religion of the time was highly critical of the knowledge systems and ideologies of its rivals. Colonial-era Indologists took Jainism for a sect of Buddhism because of similar iconography and ascetic practice. Later scholarship found the teachings different: Winternitz notes that Mahavira taught a very elaborate belief in the soul, which Buddhists denied.

Later debates within Jainism also look back to him. The Digambaras hold that a woman cannot gain liberation through asceticism and can at best be reborn as a man, while the Śvetāmbaras read him as encouraging both sexes to pursue moksha. The two sects differ on where he preached, on his marriage, and on the embryo transfer.

Historians doubt the traditional chronology. The Vira Nirvana Samvat count rests on a list of kings that Rapson calls unreliable, as it confuses rulers of Ujjain, Magadha and other kingdoms. Paul Dundas also cautions that anekantavada has been misread as general religious tolerance: it concerns the nature of reality, and the five vows for monks and nuns carry no 'perhaps'.
sections.last:
Jain texts place his nirvana at Pawapuri in present-day Bihar. The Śvētāmbara tradition dates it to 527 BCE and the Digambara tradition to 510 BCE, and in both his jiva is believed to dwell in Siddhashila, the home of liberated souls. His chief disciple, Gautama, is said to have attained omniscience the night Mahavira reached nirvana.

Accounts differ. Some texts describe a simple nirvana, and others recount grand celebrations attended by gods and kings. In Jinasena's Mahapurana heavenly beings arrive to perform the funeral rites. Some texts say that at the age of 72 he gave his last preaching over six days to a large crowd, which fell asleep and woke to find him gone, leaving only his nails and hair, which his followers cremated. The Digambara Pravachanasara holds that only the nails and hair of Tirthankaras remain, and the rest of the body dissolves in the air like camphor.

Historians date his death differently. On the Buddha's short chronology, Dundas suggests that Mahavira may have died around 425 BCE or a few years after, and Long suggests a lifespan of c. 499 to 427 BCE. Others, using Hemachandra's chronologies, give 549 BCE for his birth and 477 or c. 468 to 467 BCE for his death.
sections.legacy:
Mahavira's legacy is the codification of Jain philosophy and the four-fold order of monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen, which gave both ascetics and householders a path and let Jainism survive as a living tradition. Jain tradition says that the teachings were gradually lost after about 300 BCE, when a famine in Magadha dispersed the monks. Later efforts to gather the canon, including an attempt in the 5th century CE, did not reconcile the Śvetāmbara and Digambara versions, and each tradition holds a somewhat different and incomplete one. The texts were first written on palm leaf: the Ṣaṭkhaṅḍāgama, among the oldest Digambara texts, was written down under Āchārya Dharasena.

He is among the five Tirthankaras who attract the most devotional worship. His emblem is the lion, and his earliest images come from Mathura. Jains celebrate his birth as Mahavir Janma Kalyanak and his nirvana as Diwali, which marks the Jain New Year. Pawapuri, with its Jal Mandir, is the chief pilgrimage site.

Gandhi called Mahavira the greatest authority on ahimsa, and Rabindranath Tagore wrote that he proclaimed that religion is a reality and not a mere social convention.

summary: Mahavira, called Vardhamana at birth, is held by Jains to be the 24th and last Tirthankara. He taught five vows, with ahimsa first, and scholars see him as a reformer of an older Jain community, with dates that remain disputed.

John E. Cort, Jains in the World: Religious Values and Ideology in India (Oxford University Press, 2001)
Lawrence A. Babb, Absent Lord: Ascetics and Kings in a Jain Ritual Culture (University of California Press, 1996)
Naomi Appleton, Narrating Karma and Rebirth: Buddhist and Jain Multi-Life Stories (Cambridge University Press, 2014)
notes: Dates: traditional 599 BCE birth, 527 (Svetambara) or 510 (Digambara) BCE death; scholars propose later dates. I used the traditional dates with circa on both years.

Age at renunciation: the article says 28 in some accounts and 30 in others; kept both. The article gives 12 years in one place and 12.5 years in others for his asceticism; I used 'twelve and a half' in the first mention, 'twelve' where the omniscience passage says so.
The legacy section states the Jain tradition's account of lost teachings as tradition. Michael Hart's ranking and the temple list were left out.
